title: The Gayatri at dawn
hook: Rama woken for the dawn prayer; sandhya
carry: sandhya: the gayatri, kept at dawn

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hare Krishna, Chaitanya's song in the street. Your line was sankirtan: God's name, sung together. Today, a quieter verse, and a teacher who wakes a prince before sunrise.

Before dawn, on the steps down to the river at Varanasi, a man stands waist-deep in the water, facing east. He cups water in his hands, and as the first edge of the sun comes up, he lifts it and says a few lines under his breath. Far away in New Jersey, a boy with a new thread across his chest sets an alarm for the same hour. Same words, far older than either of them: the Gayatri. You learned on day three what it asks for. Today, why it's kept at dawn.
screen: `A MAN IN THE RIVER, FACING EAST.` → `A BOY SETS AN ALARM.` → `WHY DAWN?`

segments.voice: The Ramayana has a quiet moment that shows it. The sage Vishvamitra, the seer tradition credits with the Gayatri, has taken two boys from the palace, Rama and his brother Lakshmana. They sleep on a riverbank. Before sunrise the old sage bends over them and wakes them, in a verse that still opens the morning song at many temples: Rama, Kausalya's blessed son, the eastern sandhya, the dawn, is coming. Get up; the day's rites to the gods are waiting. And the princes rise, bathe in the river, offer water, and do their japa. Many teachers say what they chanted was the Gayatri. Here's the teaching. Did you hear the word? Sandhya: the junction, where night meets day, and the name of the dawn prayer itself. Traditionally the Gayatri is given to a child at the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, and from then on it's kept at the junctions of the day: facing the rising sun, offering water from cupped hands, asking the sun's light to wake the mind. Traditions differ on who chants it. Many keep it for those who have received the thread; many modern teachers and movements open it to everyone. Both views are held by devout Hindus; its meaning in English belongs to anyone. Now notice Rama. In the tradition he's God born human, and still his teacher wakes him in the dark to pray. The Gayatri isn't saved for a crisis. It's kept like a promise, at the same hour, before anything else gets the mind. Sandhya: the Gayatri, kept at dawn.
screen: `RAMA, THE DAWN IS COMING.` · `THE PRINCES RISE AND PRAY.` · `SANDHYA: WHERE NIGHT MEETS DAY.` · `WHO CHANTS IT: TRADITIONS DIFFER.` · then, large: `SANDHYA: THE GAYATRI, KEPT AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Sit facing a window if you can, or picture the sun just coming up. If your tradition welcomes you to chant it, say the last line softly, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat; if not, hold its meaning in English: light, illuminate the mind. Say it once, then hold it the way you'd hold your face toward the morning sun, and say it again when your attention drifts.
The Gayatri. A verse to the sun who stirs everything awake, kept at the junctions of the day, asking it to light up our minds.
Carry this: sandhya, the Gayatri, kept at dawn. Even Rama got up in the dark for it. That's day one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Many Hindus chant the Gayatri at dawn and dusk as part of sandhya worship, often facing the sun and offering water; traditionally it is taught at the upanayana (sacred thread) ceremony, while many modern teachers and movements share it with all.

notes: IMPORTANT: The Gayatri is quoted in full in transliteration. Many traditions restrict its chanting to those who have received upanayana; others (e.g. Arya Samaj, many modern teachers) teach it to all. The script presents both views without ranking and offers an English alternative. A Keeper must decide whether the full Sanskrit should be spoken in the app.
Attribution to Vishvamitra and the dating 'three thousand years' (Rig Veda book 3 is among the older family books, c. 1500–1000 BCE). Confirm or soften.

The vyahritis (bhur bhuvah svah) are prefixed in practice (from the Taittiriya Aranyaka / Yajur Veda usage); they are not in RV 3.62.10 itself. Confirm framing 'the three words most people say before it'.
Translation of the last line ('may it stir, may it light up, our minds') is the writer's paraphrase; no pre-1929 translation quoted. Confirm.
